newsitem.title: USA: Slain beauty pageant winner's half-brother not suspect.
newsitem.headline: Slain beauty pageant winner's half-brother not suspect.

text.p: Police investigating the murder of 6-year-old JonBenet Ramsey have eliminated her older half-brother as well as an older half-sister as suspects, official said Thursday.

"John Andrew and Melinda (Ramsey) are being publicly cleared of involvement in this case to relieve them of stress caused by inappropriate speculation," police spokesman Kelvin McNeill told a weekly briefing.
Last week Boulder County District Attorney Alex Hunter said detectives were looking into the alibi of John Andrew Ramsey, 20, who attends college in Colorado.
No other individuals have been ruled out as suspects in the 10-week old investigation.
The family has said John Andrew was in Atlanta days before the murder and was enroute to Michigan to meet the family Dec. 26 when he was notified the 6-year-old beauty pageant winner had been killed.
NBC news reported Thursday that it has learned that a final analysis of the father's handwriting shows it did not match a ransom note found at the house the morning of the murder.

NBC also reported that DNA evidence now being tested at Cellmark Diagnostics commercial laboratory in Maryland includes tissue found beneath the little girl's fingernails. NBC also said that contrary to earlier reports no semen was found on the girl's body or her clothing.
JonBenet Ramsey's body was found Dec. 26 by her father in the basement of their home in Boulder eight hours after the mother said she had found the ransom note demanding $118,000.

McNeill also told reporters that police have received a third handwriting sample from the slain child's mother, Patricia Ramsey. The first two samples were apparently not sufficient because the mother had been taking medication.
McNeill said police are still trying to schedule a formal interview with the parents, but have been unable to do so.
The Ramseys have offered to talk to police if they are interviewed together, away from the police station and if a doctor is present.
McNeill said Boulder police procedures call for a person to be interviewd alone. The interview must be videotaped or audiotaped and the interviewee is allowed to have only a lawyer present.
McNeill noted that people have the right not to speak with the police.

When asked about published reports that Ramsey family private investigators were looking into the background of Boulder police, he said such a step would be "entirely irrelevant" and that police would not be distracted.
